title: Workshops & Consulting
text:
Workshops & Consulting



Most AI initiatives stall not because the technology fails, but because the questions around it go unasked. What does this system actually change about how decisions get made? How do you know whether it’s working? Who’s accountable when it isn’t?


I run workshops and provide subject-matter expertise to corporate teams, executive audiences, and federal grant teams. Engagements are designed to be substantive rather than promotional: participants leave with frameworks they can use, not slogans.





Featured Offerings





A workshop on how agentic AI systems differ from chatbots and copilots, what they can and can’t reliably do today, and how to design workflows that take advantage of agency without inheriting its failure modes. Adaptable from a half-day executive briefing to a multi-day applied workshop.







Foundational machine learning and AI literacy for non-technical decision-makers. Builds enough conceptual depth to ask the right questions of vendors, data scientists, and internal teams — without pretending to turn participants into ML engineers.







A structured review of how AI is being used in an organization’s decision processes — surfacing the assumptions, failure modes, and governance gaps that tend to accumulate quietly once a system is deployed.




Also Available



A workshop on how AI changes the way teams work, communicate, and assign credit, drawing on research on advice utilization, algorithmic appreciation, and the valuation of AI-augmented work.



Network methods for surfacing coordination patterns, knowledge bottlenecks, and informal influence structures that org charts miss.



Methodological and substantive expertise for grant proposals involving human-AI teaming, computational social science, or quantitative research design.






Workshops can be tailored to industry, audience seniority, and time available. Most engagements start with a 30-minute call to scope.

title: Research
text:
Research



My current research interests lie broadly in the domain of computational social science, with three complementary areas of emphasis. A unifying thread is the use of novel computational and statistical tools to understand how people, groups, and technologies interact over time.


Copies of any of the papers below are available on request — just email me.





How do hundreds or thousands of loosely coupled contributors get anything done together? My work on this question focuses on open-source software projects, digital platforms, and open innovation communities — settings where formal authority is thin, participation is voluntary, and coordination has to emerge from the interaction patterns themselves. I use relational event models, network analysis, and mixture models to characterize how task allocation, knowledge brokerage, and core-periphery dynamics shape what these communities produce.

Representative work: Lindberg et al. (2024, MIS Quarterly) on the entrainment of task allocation cycles in open-source development; Mattarelli et al. (2025, Research Policy) on secondhand social capital and idea quality in open innovation communities; Brunswicker & Schecter (2019, Research Policy) on the paradox of change for developers’ digital innovation trajectories.




As AI systems move from tools to teammates, the interesting questions stop being about whether algorithms outperform humans and start being about how the joint system actually behaves — when people accept advice, when they over-rely, how the presence of an AI collaborator changes how work is judged by outsiders, and how disclosure and attribution shape that judgment. I run experiments and field studies on these dynamics, with a particular focus on the gap between how creators evaluate AI-augmented work and how external evaluators do.

Representative work: Panda Kumar Sachin & Schecter (2024, JAIS) on advice utilization in human-algorithm decision-making; Bogert, Schecter, & Watson (2021, Scientific Reports) on algorithmic reliance and task difficulty; Schecter et al. (2023, Computers in Human Behavior) introducing Vero, a low-tech method for studying human-AI collaboration.




The substantive questions in the first two streams kept running into methodological gaps, so I work on closing them. This stream develops and extends methods for analyzing relational event sequences (including mixture variants that recover latent behavioral archetypes), for doing valid statistical inference when key variables are themselves outputs of machine learning models, and for surfacing constructs from unstructured text in ways researchers can defend.

Representative work: Schecter, Nohadani, & Contractor (2022, MIS Quarterly) on robust inference for decision-making in networks; Schecter & Li (2026, Information Systems Research) on robust optimization for inference with ML-generated variables; Schecter & Quintane (2021, Organizational Research Methods) on the power and precision of the relational event model.




Featured Project


Once an AI system is used at one stage of a workflow, its influence rarely stays put. A model’s output becomes a colleague’s input; an annotation becomes training data; a recommendation becomes a default.
With Benjamin Richardson and Panda Kumar Sachin, I’m tracing how these imprints propagate through algorithmic ecosystems — how appreciation, aversion, and trust generalize across systems, and what that means for organizations trying to govern AI use without locking themselves into the first model they tried.

Office


C419 Benson Hall
630 S. Lumpkin St.
Athens, GA 30602
Office hours by appointment




A Note for Specific Audiences



I take students through Terry’s MIS doctoral program. Strong candidates typically have quantitative training (statistics, computer science, engineering, or a quantitative social science), some research exposure, and a substantive interest in one or more of my research streams.
The best way to gauge fit is to read a recent paper of mine and tell me what you’d do differently. Generic interest emails are fine, but specific ones get specific answers.





Briefly describe your organization, audience, and what you’re hoping to accomplish. Most engagements start with a 30-minute call to scope. See workshops & consulting for current offerings.





Happy to talk to journalists about human-AI collaboration, algorithmic decision-making, computational social science, or open-source software dynamics.





I’m always interested in conversations with researchers working on adjacent problems — relational and sequential data methods, human-AI teaming, large-group coordination, or the methodology of measuring AI’s effects on work. Email with a sentence or two on what you’re working on.

title: Home
text:
Aaron Schecter, Ph.D.



Get in touch → Download CV





I’m an Associate Professor of Management Information Systems at the University of Georgia’s Terry College of Business, where I direct the AI for Business certificate program and serve as a Faculty Fellow at UGA’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence. I work at the intersection of computational social science, human-AI collaboration, and quantitative methods — studying how groups, individuals, and increasingly capable machines coordinate, decide, and create together.
My research has appeared in MIS Quarterly, Information Systems Research, Research Policy, and others, and has been supported by the Army Research Office, Army Research Lab, and NASA. I currently serve as an Associate Editor at MIS Quarterly and as an Associate Committee Chair for ACM CHI.

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching



I teach at all three levels — doctoral, master’s/MBA, and undergraduate — and direct Terry’s AI for Business certificate program. My courses focus on the questions students will actually face once they leave: how to scope an AI project, how to evaluate whether it’s working, and how to think clearly about what the technology does and doesn’t change.


Course materials (syllabi, slides, sample assignments) are available on request — just email me.


Currently Teaching


MIST 5460


Undergraduate



A new undergraduate course I developed at UGA covering the design, deployment, and governance of agentic AI systems in business contexts. Students learn how to scope tasks, build and orchestrate AI agents, and reason about reliability, evaluation, and risk in production settings.




MIST 9770


Doctoral Seminar



Doctoral seminar covering quantitative research design, measurement, causal inference, and the analysis of complex (sequential, relational, multilevel) data structures. Emphasizes the methodological judgment that separates defensible empirical claims from confident-sounding ones.





Director


Terry’s undergraduate certificate equipping business students with practical AI literacy — covering machine learning fundamentals, generative AI, agentic systems, and the organizational and ethical questions that come with deploying these technologies at scale.
